arms.title: What Happens During the Milky Way Andromeda Collision?
Andromeda Is Already Coming (And Almost No Stars Will Collide)

source_plate.credit: NASA, ESA, J. Dalcanton, B.F. Williams, L.C. Johnson (University of Washington), the PHAT team, and R. Gendler

supporting_lines.quote: A second Milky Way is already in the sky — and it’s getting closer.
Not tomorrow. Not a Hollywood smash. But on a clock we can measure: Andromeda is inbound, and the night sky you know will not survive the meeting.
Andromeda is approaching at roughly one hundred and ten kilometres a second.
Orbit witnesses two disks slide through each other — and almost nothing hits.

supporting_lines.claim: (And Almost No Stars Will Collide) / NO CRASH
supporting_lines.quote: Because a star is a bright speck in an ocean of empty. The average gaps are so large that two galaxies can pass through one another while most suns miss by light-years. Gravity rearranges the orbits. Gas clouds can slam, spark, and light new stars under radiation and shock. Suddenly the drama is not billiard-ball smash — it’s a gravity dance through empty gaps. Star-on-star crashes stay rare — a footnote, not the fireworks.
Honest answer: probably not by a star ploughing into the Sun. Stars rarely collide.
Not as a crash. As a quiet smudge — the Andromeda Galaxy — a whole island of stars, close enough that its photons reach your eyes after a journey of about two and a half million light-years.

Then the paradox lands: approach is real; the exact merger date is still being sharpened. We measure the inbound speed — yet the exact future orbit still hides in measurement error. A merger still sits in many futures — but the timing may stretch later, and some orbits may never deliver a hard smash.
Then we need to stop thinking “crash”… and start thinking “rewrite.”
